title: User guide
intro: Welcome to {{product}}, powered by the VulnScanner engine. This guide walks you through every module so you know exactly what each one does — and what it does not do. Scan checks ports, DNS/TLS, and known CVEs on a target you control; it is a point-in-time snapshot, not 24/7 SIEM. Guard gives you agent inventory and critical alerts on enrolled hosts — it is thin, not a full Wazuh deployment. SIEM lets you search those events and open a case (an incident ticket in this app). Host Protect runs on-box web malware detection via a helper on your VPS. Button labels below match the UI exactly. No production hosts, IPs, or credentials appear here — only test assets you are authorized to scan.
mulai1: Open the app login page. No account yet? Register via <ui>Register</ui> — all you need is an email and a password.
mulai2: Verify your email if prompted (check your inbox for the link, or use the <ui>Verify email</ui> flow in the app). Unverified accounts usually cannot start scans.
mulai3: Log in. You should see your credit balance in the header and the full navigation in the sidebar — Dashboard, scanners, Schedules, Guard, Host Protect, and more.
mulai4: If your account belongs to more than one organization, pick the active workspace in the org switcher (top of the page or sidebar). Every scan and schedule you create binds to the <ui>active org</ui>, so double-check you are in the right one.
mulai5: Open <dash>Dashboard</dash> for a quick overview of recent scans and handy shortcuts.
ip1: Sidebar → <ip>IP Scanner</ip>. The page title reads <ui>IP scanner</ui>.
ip2: Check the credit preview on the form — it shows how much this IP scan costs. If your balance is low, top up first (see the Credits section below).
ip3: Fill in Target IP address — an IPv4 you control. Optionally adjust the Port range (default 1-1000, or specify individual ports like 22,80,443).
ip4: Click Start IP scan. You will see Initializing scan… and then get redirected to Scan details (/scan/:id).
ip5: Watch the status badge: <ui>pending</ui> → <ui>running</ui> → <ui>completed</ui> (or <ui>failed</ui>). If you stay on the scanner page, a <ui>Scan progress</ui> card may also update in real time.
ip6: Once the status is <ui>completed</ui>, head to <hasil>Read results & download</hasil> to see what was found.
ipNote: What you get: open ports and services (via nmap), known CVEs from OSV.dev, severity ratings, and OS fingerprint when available. A completed scan is a snapshot of that moment — it is not a SOC watching your host around the clock. It will not catch business-logic flaws (OWASP WSTG category) that need a human tester to explore.
dom2: Fill in <ui>Target domain</ui> — a hostname you own. The optional <ui>Try example.com</ui> button is just for testing the UI flow; do not treat those public-lab results as a real production audit.
dom3: Check the credit cost, then click <ui>Start domain scan</ui>.
dom4: Follow the redirect to the scan detail page and wait for <ui>completed</ui>.
domNote: What you get: DNS records and subdomain enumeration, TLS certificate analysis, security headers audit, and technology fingerprinting. This is not a pentest of login flows or payment logic — it covers the publicly visible surface.
mob1: Sidebar → <mob>Mobile Scanner</mob>. Look for the <ui>Upload binary</ui> card.
mob2: Pick your platform: Android or iOS. Android accepts .apk or .aab files. iOS accepts .ipa. Max file size follows what the UI shows (typically hundreds of MB).
mob3: Drag-and-drop the file onto the upload area, or click to browse. The file extension must match the platform you selected.
mob4: Check your credits — apk and ipa scans are billed separately — then start the upload from the form.
mob5: After the job is created, open <ui>Scan details</ui> and wait for it to finish.
mobNote: What you get: manifest and permission analysis, exported component detection, hardcoded secret scanning, and platform-specific binary checks.
res1: On the <ui>Scan details</ui> page you will find the severity summary, the <ui>Findings</ui> table, and the <ui>Scan info</ui> card (timestamp, target, scan type). If the status is completed but findings are empty, that means the engine genuinely found nothing in that pass — it does not mean the host is "secure forever."
res2: If the scan came from a recurring schedule, look for the baseline diff strip showing new and resolved findings compared to the previous run.
res3: Download reports from the buttons in the top-right corner:
resJson: <ui>JSON</ui> — raw scan data for your own tooling
res4: Need to scan a similar target again? Click <ui>Re-scan</ui> to jump back to the matching scanner form.
res5: Scan history is also available on the Dashboard — click any row to open the same detail view.
jadIntro: Quick note: the <ui>viewer</ui> role is read-only and cannot create or edit schedules. If you are an org admin, member, or owner, read on.
jad1: Sidebar → <sch>Schedules</sch>. The page title is <ui>Jadwal scan</ui>.
jad2: Check <ui>Kuota jadwal aktif</ui> (e.g. 3/10). If the quota is full, disable an old schedule before creating a new one.
jad3: On the <ui>Jadwal baru</ui> card, fill in:
jadLabel: <ui>Label</ui> — optional, a friendly name for this schedule
jadTarget: <ui>Target</ui> — the IP or domain to scan (required)
jadEmail: <ui>Email notifikasi</ui> — optional; defaults to your account email
jad4: Click <ui>Buat jadwal</ui>. The new schedule appears under <ui>Jadwal Anda</ui>.
jad5: For each schedule row you can: <ui>Aktifkan</ui> / <ui>Nonaktifkan</ui> it, download the <ui>Eksekutif</ui> report from the last run, open <ui>scan terakhir</ui> / <ui>buka scan</ui> in the run history, or delete it entirely.
jad6: Each scheduled run deducts personal credits. If your balance hits zero, the schedule may disable itself with a credits error — so keep an eye on your balance.
aIntro: Assets are named IP or domain targets for your workspace, with a per-SKU hard cap (Basic: 1, Pro: 3, Multi: 10). Use assets so that schedules and pack exports reference a stable name instead of raw IPs — think of it as a lightweight target registry, not a full CMDB.
a1: Sidebar → <as>Assets</as>. The page title is <ui>Assets</ui>. Check the SKU quota line (current count / limit).
a2: Click <ui>Add asset</ui> (or <ui>Add your first asset</ui> if the list is empty). Fill in <ui>Name</ui>, <ui>Target</ui>, <ui>Type</ui> (IP or domain), optional <ui>Notes</ui>, then <ui>Save</ui>.
a3: Per row: click <ui>Create schedule</ui> (weekly by default) if the asset does not have one yet; or <ui>Delete</ui> if you no longer need it. If the cap is full, remove an old asset first.
a4: Optional: <ui>Download pack JSON</ui> for an org-scoped export of all named targets. Do not put production IPs into public tickets or screenshots.
ws1: Open <ws>Workspace</ws> (or workspace settings in the navigation).
ws2: <ui>Buat organisasi</ui>: fill in <ui>Nama</ui>, optionally a <ui>Slug</ui>, then click <ui>Buat workspace</ui>. You become the owner automatically.
ws3: Switch the active org using the switcher so that scans and schedules land in the correct workspace.
ws4: Owner or admin: invite team members by email and assign a role (member / viewer / admin as shown in the UI), then send the invite. Track status in the invite list; invites can be revoked at any time.
ws5: Invitee: open the invite link (a URL containing a token) → the <ui>Terima undangan</ui> card appears → click <ui>Terima undangan</ui> while logged in to accept.
ws6: Check the Anggota list to see everyone and their roles. Note: a platform admin (is_admin) is not the same as an org admin — the global /admin panel is a separate level of access.
cr1: Your current balance is always visible in the header (the Credits chip).
cr2: Before you start a scan, the form shows a cost preview. The start button is disabled if you do not have enough credits.
cr3: After a scan completes, check <ch>Credit History</ch> for the deduction — and note that failed scans often trigger an automatic refund.
cr4: Top-up in v1 works via invoice through your account manager or ops team — there is no in-app card payment form yet. Contact AM/ops if your balance is empty.
cr5: Important: credits are <ui>personal</ui> to your user account, not a shared org wallet.
gIntro: Guard gives your organization an inventory of enrolled agents and a feed of critical alerts from those hosts. It is not a full SIEM, not a raw-log dashboard, and not a vulnerability scanner. Think of it this way: OpenVAS-style scanners check what is exposed on a target; Guard watches what is running on a host you already enrolled. This module is the thin agent side — lightweight inventory plus high-severity alerts, not a full Wazuh deployment with dashboards and SOAR playbooks. Only org admins and owners can enable Guard or create enrollment tokens. The host setup steps below use placeholders (no lab or production addresses in this public doc).
g2: The <ui>Status</ui> card shows your active org. If Guard is <ui>nonaktif</ui>, an admin clicks <ui>Aktifkan Guard</ui> to turn it on. The module status will show <ui>nyala</ui> (on) or <ui>nonaktif</ui> (off).
g3: Once Guard is on, the admin sees a <ui>Token enroll</ui> card. Optionally add a label, then click <ui>Buat token</ui>. Copy the raw token immediately — it is shown only once. The UI also displays a <ui>Langkah host (setelah token)</ui> block with a curl example you can run on the target host. Never paste enrollment tokens into public chat or repositories.
gHostLead: On the target host (a machine you legally control), follow this order:
gCurlLead: Example enrollment from the host (replace the app origin and token; no JWT needed):
gEndpoint: The public org-bound endpoint uses a token (not JWT): POST /api/guard/enroll with body { token, agent_name }. The response includes agent_id, agent_key, manager_host, and install_hint.
gInstallLead: Agent runtime install on the target host — install wazuh-agent using the commands for your distro below (no lab secrets included):
gHostCmds: Commands on the target host (by distro)
g7: Click <ui>Sinkronkan</ui> (admin only) to refresh the agent projection. The <ui>Agen</ui> table shows each agent's status (online / disconnected / pending), and the <ui>Alert kritis</ui> section shows high-severity events.
g8: Viewer and above can see agents and alerts after Guard is enabled, but only admin/owner can generate enrollment tokens.
g9: Quick troubleshooting: if enrollment returns 4xx, the token is expired, revoked, or belongs to a different org. If an agent stays pending too long, check that the host can reach manager_host from the enrollment response, then click Sync. Never use Manager passwords on the enrolled host.
sIntro: SIEM is a separate module from Guard. It gives you a controlled search interface for security events (not the full Wazuh Discover or dashboard experience) and lets you open cases — structured incident tickets — right inside the app. A scheduled IP or domain scan does not feed this page; SIEM events come from enrolled agents. The environment flag SIEM_ENABLED must be on; if it is off, the page will tell you the module is inactive.
s1: Make sure you have agents enrolled in <g>Guard</g> first. Without any agents in the org, SIEM will show empty results.
s2: Open Sidebar → <siem>SIEM</siem>. Use the filters: time range (WIB), minimum severity level, agent, and a free-text search box, then click <ui>Terapkan</ui>.
s3: Click any result row to see the projected event detail (not raw logs). Members and above can <ui>Buat kasus</ui> (create a case) directly from an event.
s4: Owners and admins can change a case's status: <ui>terbuka</ui> (open) → <ui>diakui</ui> (acknowledged) → <ui>ditutup</ui> (closed). Members and above can add notes to a case (but not dump raw logs into it).
sCasesWhat: The Kasus (Cases) tab is an incident ticket in this app — not a Wazuh plugin and not the same as the Guard critical-alert list. Events stay in the search indexer and you pull them on demand. A case stores a title, status, linked event IDs, an assignee, and notes — all in Postgres, all inside Sinexis.
sCasesVs: Use Cari event when you need to answer "what happened?" — filter by rule, agent, time, severity level. Use Kasus when the answer is "we are working this until it is resolved." Guard still only surfaces critical alerts (level ≥ 12); SIEM search can go lower so you catch the full picture.
sCasesFlow: Select an event row → click <ui>Buat kasus</ui> → open the <ui>Kasus</ui> tab to link more events and add investigation notes. The status flow is: <ui>terbuka</ui> → <ui>diakui</ui> → <ui>ditutup</ui>. Viewers can read cases; members and above can create and comment; owners and admins can close or reassign.
sCasesNot: Cases are not SOAR automation, not a Wazuh dashboard, and not scan findings. The page copy says it plainly: cases live in this app, not in the Wazuh cases plugin.
uIntro: Uptime runs outside-in HTTP and TCP checks against targets in your workspace, subject to a per-SKU seat cap. It is completely separate from Guard, SIEM, and scan schedules — think of it as a simple availability monitor. The flag UPTIME_ENABLED is on by default; if the page says the module is inactive, ops has turned it off in this environment.
u1: Sidebar → <up>Uptime</up>. The page title is <ui>Uptime</ui>. Check the SKU line for your current enabled count versus the limit.
u2: Click <ui>Add monitor</ui> (or <ui>Add your first monitor</ui>). Fill in <ui>Name</ui>, <ui>Target</ui> (a URL or host:port), <ui>Type</ui> (HTTP or TCP), <ui>Interval (seconds)</ui>, and optionally a <ui>Keyword</ui> to match in the response and a <ui>Notify email</ui> for alerts, then <ui>Save</ui>.
u3: Watch the state badges: <ui>up</ui> / <ui>down</ui> / <ui>unknown</ui>. Per row you can <ui>Pause</ui> / <ui>Resume</ui> or <ui>Delete</ui>. If the seat cap is full, pause or delete an old monitor before adding a new one.
u4: Down/up email notifications are best-effort — SMTP must be configured by your ops team. Never put raw monitor IPs on a public status page; the mapping uses display names only.
spIntro: Each org can publish one public status page, driven by Uptime monitors. Incidents are posted manually by your team — this is a communication tool, not an auto-detect system. Publishing requires org SKU pro or multi. A custom hostname is multi only. TLS for customer-hosted domains goes through Cloudflare for SaaS — the app does not run ACME certificate issuance.
sp1: Create at least one Uptime monitor first (see the previous section).
sp2: Sidebar → <sp>Status page</sp>. If no page exists yet, fill in <ui>Slug</ui> and <ui>Title</ui>, then click <ui>Create page</ui>.
sp3: Add component: pick a Monitor, set a public Display name (never the raw URL or IP), and save. Then click Publish. The public URL is /status/{slug} on the platform host.
sp4: Post a <ui>New incident</ui> with an impact level and status, then add <ui>Update</ui> entries as the situation evolves. <ui>Unpublish</ui> hides the public page when you no longer need it.
sp5: Custom hostname (Multi SKU only): fill in <ui>Custom hostname</ui>, point a CNAME record at the documented target, then click <ui>Verify DNS</ui>. Do not expect the app to issue certificates for your custom domain.
hpIntro: Host Protect scans web files for malware directly on your VPS — it runs on the box, not on a SaaS worker somewhere in the cloud. It requires a Guard-enrolled host. Scan jobs are triggered by the Host Protect helper (a systemd timer plus a token), which polls the API and runs YARA/ClamAV rules against your web root. This is not Imunify, not Guard alerts, and not SIEM search. Quarantine isolates a suspicious file so it cannot execute; it does not reconstruct or restore your site — that is a separate ops task. If you see a status like <ui>completed (1 hits)</ui> with a note about hidden hits, it means the helper ran successfully and reported a count. The hits are real detections from rules on your host, not something invented in the cloud.
hp1: Start in Guard: copy the agent UUID for the host you want to protect. An admin then generates a Host Protect helper token (separate from the enrollment token — shown once, keep it safe). Write that token to a mode-600 file on the VPS, for example /root/host-agent.token. You still need the enrollment fields (manager_host, agent_key) returned by POST /api/guard/enroll. After the helper starts polling, the Sidebar → Host Protect page will show data. If the page says the module is off, your ops team has not enabled Host Protect in this environment.
hpGet: On the VPS, download one file — the installer script itself, not a GitHub web page. Click sinexis-install.sh and use your browser's Save function, or paste the wget command below into a terminal (the raw URL is on raw.githubusercontent.com, not the blob page). Optionally, grab a GitHub Release asset and verify its SHA256. Do not clone the repo. Do not curl | bash.
hpGetCheck: Sanity check: run head -n1 sinexis-install.sh — it must print #!/usr/bin/env bash. If you see instead, you saved the GitHub HTML page by mistake. Delete the file and run wget again using the raw URL (not a github.com/.../blob/... link).
hpInstall: On a TTY, run sudo ./sinexis-install.sh. The menu offers three options: (1) install wazuh-agent — you will need the manager_host from the enrollment response and must import the agent_key with manage_agents; (2) configure the Host Protect helper — you will need the Guard UUID and the token file; (3) both at once. For non-interactive installs, use flags: --install-wazuh-agent --manager-host HOST and/or --configure-host-protect --agent-id <UUID> --token-file /root/host-agent.token --api-base https://sinexis.app. The helper writes /etc/sinexis/host-protect.env (mode 600) and enables sinexis-host-protect@.timer via systemctl, which polls every 5 minutes. If the env file is missing, the helper exits with code 4.
hp2: Click <ui>Add site</ui> only after the helper has completed its first poll (check "last helper poll" on the agent row). Fill in <ui>Name</ui>, the <ui>Root path</ui> on the agent, the <ui>Guard agent</ui>, and optionally a CMS hint. Guard enrollment alone is not enough — scanning fails closed until the helper polls at least once. Host Protect hits are never mixed with IP or domain scan findings. Zero hits after a genuine poll is an honest empty result (no matching rules on that path), not a UI bug.
hp3: Critical finding classes (webshell, backdoor) trigger a one-time email to the site owner per new path plus rule combination. Re-scans only update the last-seen timestamp — you will not get a second email for the same hit. File contents are never attached to emails.
hp4: <ui>Quarantine</ui> / <ui>Restore</ui> / <ui>Ignore</ui> are isolate actions on the flagged file. Actually reconstructing the site (CMS restore from backup, manual cleanup) is a hybrid ops ticket — Host Protect does not rewrite or repair files for you.
hp5: Open the WAF tab. The default per-site mode is off. detect mode logs rule matches on the customer's nginx snippet without blocking. protect mode is available on Host Multi only — it sets SecRuleEngine On (403 deny) on that same customer VPS. Use Copy nginx snippet to paste the config on the customer VPS only — never paste it onto the Sinexis public edge. Simulate request is a control-plane lab tool, not live traffic interception. Optional Hourly malware scans still cap at two in-flight jobs per org.
t1: Only scan or enroll assets you legally control. Scanning third-party infrastructure without authorization is a fast way to get your account suspended.
t2: Never store passwords, API keys, or internal IP addresses in public tickets, screenshots, or shared documents.
t3: Scan attach ≠ SIEM 24/7. Guard v1 = inventory + critical alerts + enroll — not SOAR, not a customer manager dashboard. Uptime = outside-in probes, not an SLA guarantee. Status page never exposes raw monitor URL/IP. Host Protect quarantine ≠ reconstruct. Host WAF is a control plane plus a customer nginx snippet, not Coraza on sinexis.app.
